content: The interventions recommended for managing urinary incontinence are not resource-intensive. These interventions are feasible to implement and can be safely administered by family caregivers. Additionally, delivering care through non-specialist health workers has proven to be an effective model, particularly in lowand middle-income countries. Educational interventions have demonstrated feasibility and promising outcomes. Based on these findings, the guideline development group concluded that the recommendations are implementable in both highand low-resource settings. The guideline development group strongly believed that the proposed recommendations would enhance health equity. Prompted voiding is a viable management strategy for older individuals with cognitive impairment. The strength of this recommendation is conditional, and the quality of evidence supporting it is very low. Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT), either alone or combined with bladder control strategies and self-monitoring, is strongly recommended for older women experiencing urinary incontinence, including urge, stress, or mixed types. The quality of evidence supporting this recommendation is moderate. Most studies on PFMT were conducted in high-income countries, and while the majority involved older women, the recommendation may also be applicable to older men. The duration of PFMT interventions in trials ranged from 6 to 12 weeks, with most requiring daily practice. For older individuals who are bedridden or have significant mental and/or physical decline, the use of continence products should be considered. Healthcare providers should take a detailed history and inquire specifically about urinary incontinence, including the onset, symptoms, and frequency. It is important to note that at least half of women with urinary incontinence do not report the issue to their general practitioners. Therefore, healthcare professionals should routinely screen for urinary incontinence in older women and men. Clinicians should review current medications that may cause or exacerbate urinary incontinence. While pharmacological therapy can reduce symptoms and even achieve complete continence, many older individuals discontinue medications due to adverse effects. Specialist care providers should be consulted when initiating pharmacological treatment. As a first-line treatment, bladder training should be advised for a minimum of six weeks. This involves instructing older individuals to adhere to a strict schedule for bathroom visits, starting with intervals of every two hours and gradually increasing the time between visits to improve bladder control.
